# The Weight of Small Things

I find myself thinking about erasers lately. Specifically, the pink rubber kind that sat in every classroom of my childhood, worn down to nubbins by October, leaving smudges of graphite and eraser dust across margins and between lines. They never worked as well as they promised. The harder you rubbed, the worse it got. There was a technique to it—light circular motions, almost apologetic in their gentleness—but most of us never learned. We pressed hard, frustrated that our mistakes wouldn't simply vanish.

That's a metaphor for something, probably. Most things are.

I've been thinking a lot about what it means to be an adult. Not the obvious markers—the mortgage, the taxes, the resignation—but the smaller realizations that arrive without fanfare. Like how one day you stop hoping a problem will go away on its own and start researching solutions at 11 PM on a Tuesday. Like how conversations with old friends sometimes become a recitation of logistics and ailments rather than dreams. Like how you can want something genuinely and still not be willing to rearrange your life to get it.

There's no dramatic moment when this happens. You don't wake up and feel the invisible crown of responsibility placed upon your head. It just accumulates, like dust on a shelf you keep meaning to wipe down.

I watched a bird land on my window ledge today. It sat there for maybe ten seconds, completely still, as if gathering information. Then it flew away. I wondered what determined that timing. Did it sense something was wrong? Was it always going to be ten seconds, some genetic timer? I'll never know, and I've thought about it more times than is reasonable. This is the thing about being conscious—you're stuck with all these meaningless questions your brain generates like involuntary thought spam.

Someone told me recently that they've stopped watching the news because the world feels too heavy to carry. I understood that immediately. There's a particular exhaustion that comes from proximity to information you can do nothing about. You read something terrible and it becomes part of you, another stone in an invisible pocket. Enough stones and you start to sink, or at least you move differently through space, with more effort.

But I keep watching. I keep reading. I tell myself it's important to bear witness, to stay informed, to maintain some minimal connection to what's happening beyond my small life. The truth might be simpler: I'm afraid that if I stop paying attention, I'll somehow become less real. That there's value in suffering alongside others, even if it's only suffering at a distance, through a screen.

This might be absurd. Probably it is.

I've been noticing how much of adult conversation is people asking each other "how are you?" when they don't particularly want the answer. It's a greeting, not a question. If you answer honestly—really honestly, not the "good, tired" kind of honestly—people get uncomfortable. They've already moved on to the next thing. So you learn to compress your experience into a word or two, a social token that keeps the machinery of interaction running smoothly.

Sometimes I do this with myself. I ask how I am and give the abbreviated answer, without examining the question too closely. Easier that way. Less likely to come face-to-face with something I'm not equipped to handle.

I read that octopi can taste with their arms. That they have neurons distributed throughout their bodies that allow them to sense and sample the world directly, not through a centralized nervous system that files reports. There's something beautiful about that—being able to experience things immediately, without the delay of sending signals back to a central processor for analysis. Though I suppose it also means they can't separate their thinking from their feeling. Everything is direct and immediate. I'm not sure if that sounds like freedom or torture.

We were made for delayed response, we humans. We have this distance between stimulus and reaction, this gap where consciousness supposedly lives. We like to think it's our greatest achievement—this ability to pause before acting, to consider before speaking. But I wonder sometimes if we've just become very good at hiding. At creating enough space between ourselves and our lives that we can pretend we're observers rather than participants.

The thought I keep coming back to, though: what if it's enough? What if my small life, my private observations about erasers and birds and octopi, my struggling attempts to stay connected to both the world and to myself—what if that's enough?

There's no cosmic significance to it. I won't change anything. I won't solve anything. But I'll exist in the particular way that I exist, conscious and struggling and occasionally noticing beautiful or terrible things. I'll carry my stones. I'll ask questions about bird timing and never get answers. I'll keep watching the news and keep talking to friends about logistics and ailments. I'll continue to press too hard when trying to erase my mistakes, leaving smudges.

And maybe—this is the thought I'm arriving at—maybe that's what everyone is doing. Maybe we're all just walking around with our private collection of strange thoughts and impossible questions, trying to behave as if we understand what's happening, when mostly we're just reacting to circumstances we didn't choose, doing our best with limited information.

That seems less lonely somehow.

The light is changing outside my window. It's that particular slant of late afternoon that makes everything seem important and temporary at once. I won't remember this moment. By tomorrow, I'll have forgotten the bird, the specific texture of this thought. But something will remain—the impression of attention, the small fact that I was here, noticing things.

That will have to be enough.
